title: Why is the clock angle thirty degrees at one o'clock?
description: The book says that the hands of a clock make thirty degrees at one o'clock. The angle of one gap is found by sharing the full turn into twelve equal gaps, and the angles at other hours come from counting the gaps between the hands.
teaching_notes: One idea: the angle between the hands is the number of gaps between them times thirty degrees. Watch for students who forget that the hands make two angles that together fill the full turn.

source: Figure it Out: Where are the angles?, Q1
video_script.why: The child uses the full turn cut into twelve equal gaps from the solved example, to explain thirty degrees at one o'clock and to find the angles at other hours.
video_script.substitution: One o'clock, two o'clock, four o'clock and six o'clock of the book's question.
video_script.anchor: the clock face of the book with the numbers one to twelve and the two hands

final_answer.value: 30° = 360° ÷ 12; 2 o'clock 60°, 4 o'clock 120°, 6 o'clock 180°; also 3 o'clock 90°, 9 o'clock 270°
final_answer.spoken: two o'clock sixty degrees, four o'clock one hundred and twenty degrees, six o'clock one hundred and eighty degrees

maths_rules: a full turn of the clock face = 360 degrees, cut into 12 equal gaps
one gap = 360 / 12 = 30 degrees, so one o'clock gives 30 degrees
six o'clock: 6 x 30 = 180 degrees, a straight angle
nine o'clock: 9 x 30 = 270 degrees one way round, and 3 x 30 = 90 degrees the other way; 90 + 270 = 360
check: the angle one way and the angle the other way add up to 360 degrees
video_script.design: The clock face stays on the board. The angle of one gap is found first, then the gaps are counted for each hour, and the angles are held back until the answer line.
open_questions: The book gives 270 degrees for nine o'clock, which is the angle the long way round. The angle between the hands is usually taken as 90 degrees, the short way, so the video says both and that they add up to a full turn.
